name: Delhi
subtitle: City of Cities
description: Five moments in the northern Delhi triangle between the Ridge and the Yamuna, from Firoz Shah's Firozabad (1380) through Din Panah and Humayun's Tomb to Shah Jahan's walled Shahjahanabad (1660) and Bahadur Shah Zafar's city on the eve of 1857. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Yamuna
water.blurb: The Yamuna ran close under the high ground here: Firoz Shah's Kotla, Purana Qila, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort were all built on its west bank, and in 1660 it lapped the fort's river wall below the marble palaces.

water.name: Yamuna
water.blurb: By the 19th century the river had drifted east, leaving a sandy flat (the bela) between the fort wall and the water where melons were grown and the bridge of boats landed.

water.name: Salimgarh channel
water.blurb: A side arm of the Yamuna cut Salimgarh off from the mainland; Jahangir bridged it in 1622, and Shah Jahan's fort was set just south of it.

water.name: Nahr-i-Faiz (Chandni Chowk canal)
water.blurb: Ali Mardan Khan's canal, brought from the Yamuna far upstream, ran along of Chandni Chowk in a stone channel with pools and trees, then under the Lahori Gate into the fort as the Nahr-i-Bihisht. It silted up in the 18th century and was restored by the British in 1820.

water.name: Faiz Bazaar canal
water.blurb: A branch of the canal ran down the middle of Faiz Bazaar from the fort's Delhi Gate to the city's Delhi Gate.

hills.name: The Ridge
hills.blurb: The last spur of the Aravallis, a rocky quartzite ridge of thorn scrub. Firoz Shah built a hunting lodge on it; in 1857 the British army camped behind it for four months and shelled the city from its batteries at Hindu Rao's house.

hills.name: Bhojla Pahari
hills.blurb: A low outcrop of rock in the middle of Shahjahanabad, chosen for the Jama Masjid so that it stands above the roofs of the city.

roads.name: Chandni Chowk
roads.blurb: Jahanara's processional avenue from the fort's Lahori Gate to the Fatehpuri Masjid, about 1.3 km long and 40 yards wide, with the canal and shade trees down its middle and arcaded shops on both sides; named after the moonlit pool in its octagonal square.

roads.name: Faiz Bazaar
roads.blurb: The second great avenue, from the fort's Delhi Gate south to the city's Delhi Gate, laid out by Akbarabadi Begum with a canal down the centre. Daryaganj lay to its east.

roads.name: Khas Bazaar
roads.blurb: The bazaar between the Jama Masjid's east gate and the fort, where nobles' retinues waited; Urdu Bazaar ran beside it.

roads.name: Dariba Kalan
roads.blurb: The 'street of the incomparable pearl', a lane of jewellers and silversmiths from Chandni Chowk to the Jama Masjid.

roads.name: Chawri Bazaar
roads.blurb: From the Jama Masjid west to Hauz Qazi; in the 18th and 19th centuries the quarter of brass-sellers and of the courtesans' salons.

roads.name: Lal Kuan
roads.blurb: The street of the red well, from Hauz Qazi north to the Fatehpuri Masjid.

roads.name: Khari Baoli
roads.blurb: West of the Fatehpuri Masjid to the Lahori Gate, named after a brackish step-well; later the city's great spice and grain market.

roads.name: Road to Karnal and Lahore
roads.blurb: The imperial highway north to Panipat, Karnal and Lahore left Kashmiri Gate along the river past the gardens; the British Civil Lines grew along it.

roads.name: Road to Sabzi Mandi
roads.blurb: From the Lahori and Kabuli gates past the vegetable market of Sabzi Mandi and through the gap in the Ridge towards the Grand Trunk Road.

roads.name: Road to Ajmer
roads.blurb: South-west from Ajmeri Gate past Paharganj and Jaisinghpura towards Ajmer and the shrine of Muinuddin Chishti.

roads.name: Road to Mathura and Agra
roads.blurb: Out of the Delhi Gate past the ruins of Firozabad, the Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb, to Mathura and Agra: the road of every Mughal march south.

roads.name: Road to Mehrauli
roads.blurb: South-west through the old ruin-field to the Qutb and the first cities of Delhi.

roads.name: Road to Old Delhi and Jahanpanah
roads.blurb: Firozabad's road south-west to the older cities at Siri, Jahanpanah and Mehrauli, about ten miles off; Firoz lined such roads with serais and wells.

roads.name: Road to the Kushk-i-Shikar
roads.blurb: North from the Kotla through the suburbs to the sultan's hunting palace on the Ridge.

roads.name: Sher Shah's road to Agra
roads.blurb: Sher Shah rebuilt the great road from Bengal to the Indus with serais, wells and post-horses every few miles; through Delhi it ran under the walls of his fort.

walls.name: Wall of Shahjahanabad
walls.blurb: First an earthen rampart (1650), rebuilt in stone in 1651–58: about six kilometres round, with bastions every few hundred yards and fourteen gates. The British repaired and strengthened its northern face with new bastions in the early 19th century; it held them off for four months in 1857.

walls.name: Wall of Shergarh
walls.blurb: Sher Shah's city wall ran from the Purana Qila north to the Kabuli Darwaza opposite the Kotla; only its two gates survive and its line is conjectural.

walls.name: Ruined wall of Shergarh
walls.blurb: By Shah Jahan's day the Surid wall was a crumbling bank between fields, its stone taken for the new city.

bridges.name: Salimgarh bridge
bridges.blurb: Jahangir's bridge of 1622 across the channel to Salimgarh; Shah Jahan linked it to the fort, and Bahadur Shah Zafar is said to have left the fort this way in September 1857.

bridges.name: Bridge of boats
bridges.blurb: A pontoon bridge on moored boats carried the road to Meerut across the Yamuna below Salimgarh; on 11 May 1857 the mutineers from Meerut rode over it into Delhi.

blocks.name: Farrash Khana and Kucha Pati Ram
Sita Ram Bazaar and Hauz Qazi
Serai and houses outside Delhi Gate

gardens.name: Firoz Shah's gardens by the Ridge
Tomb garden by the Mathura road
Orchards west of the Mathura road

marsh.name: The bela below Kotla and Purana Qila

districts.name: Firozabad
districts.description: Firoz Shah's capital, founded 1354: not a walled town but a string of mohallas, eighteen villages and gardens round the Kotla, said by his chronicler Afif to stretch five kos along the river, with eight public mosques.

districts.name: Din Panah and Shergarh
districts.description: Humayun's 'refuge of the faith' (1533) on the old mound of Indarpat, refounded by Sher Shah as Shergarh with a citadel and a city wall reaching north to the Kabuli Darwaza.

districts.name: Ghiyaspur
districts.description: The village round the khanqah of Nizamuddin Auliya (d. 1325), where pilgrims, qawwals and the dead of every dynasty gather; now Nizamuddin Basti.

districts.name: Daryaganj
districts.description: The riverside quarter east of Faiz Bazaar, of nobles' mansions on the water; from 1803 the first British cantonment, later a quarter of bungalows and old havelis.

districts.name: Chandni Chowk
districts.description: The commercial heart of Shahjahanabad: the avenue, its katras and kuchas, the bankers' and jewellers' lanes of Dariba and Kinari Bazaar.

districts.name: Civil Lines
districts.description: North of Kashmiri Gate along the river: the bungalows of British officials (Ludlow Castle, Metcalfe House) in large walled compounds, built after the troops moved out to the Ridge in 1828.

districts.name: Paharganj
districts.description: The 'hill market' outside Ajmeri Gate, the city's wholesale grain market under the Mughals.

districts.name: Sabzi Mandi
districts.description: The vegetable market and gardens outside the Kabuli and Lahori gates, in 1857 a no-man's-land of walled gardens fought over between the city and the Ridge.

periods.label: Firozabad
periods.summary: Firoz Shah Tughlaq has left the old hill cities to the south and built Firozabad on the Yamuna: a palace-citadel, the Kotla, with a stepped pavilion crowned by an Ashokan pillar he had floated down the river, mosques of rubble and lime plaster, hunting lodges on the Ridge. A spread of mohallas, gardens and villages rather than a walled city, ruled by an old, pious sultan.
periods.feel: Lime kilns and rubble masons, the river slapping at the Kotla's ghats, the call to prayer from rough grey domes.

houses.title: Mohallas of Firozabad
houses.text: Rubble-and-mud houses round small courts, one or two storeys, flat roofs of earth on timber, whitewashed lime plaster on the better ones. Lanes bend between them to a mosque and a well; the sultan's nobles have walled compounds with gardens.

outskirts.title: Gardens and villages
outskirts.text: Mud-walled villages, orchards watered from wells by bullock-wheels, Firoz's new gardens and the scattered tombs of earlier sultans' men.

periods.label: Din Panah and Shergarh
periods.summary: Humayun founded Din Panah, 'refuge of the faith', on the ancient mound of Indarpat in 1533; Sher Shah Sur drove him out in 1540, rebuilt the citadel in grey quartzite and red sandstone and laid out a larger city, Shergarh, reaching north to the Kotla. Sher Shah's mosque in the fort is the finest building of its day. Firozabad is half-abandoned and quarried for stone.
periods.feel: Masons dressing red sandstone at the gates, horsemen of the royal post on the Agra road, a city that has changed masters twice in ten years.

houses.title: Houses of Shergarh
houses.text: Rubble and brick courtyard houses with flat roofs, a few of the richer with red sandstone door frames, packed along the roads from the fort gates. Many are new-built on old Firozabad foundations with stone carted from the ruins.

outskirts.title: Ruins and villages
outskirts.text: Fields among the ruined mohallas of Firozabad, grazing on the riverbank, the village round Nizamuddin's shrine.

periods.label: Humayun's Tomb
periods.summary: Humayun died in the Purana Qila in 1556; his widow Haji Begum built his tomb by Nizamuddin's shrine, the first great garden-tomb of India, in red sandstone and white marble, finished about 1572. Akbar rules from Agra, so Delhi is a provincial city of courtiers' tombs, mosques and serais; Maham Anga's madrasa faces the fort, and the Arab Sarai houses Haji Begum's dependants, by tradition Arabs.
periods.feel: Quiet after the court has gone: pilgrims to the shrine, Persian masons' chisels at the tomb, the old fort's gates locked at dusk.

houses.title: Houses round the old fort
houses.text: Flat-roofed rubble and brick houses round courts, two storeys at most, along the roads between the Purana Qila, Nizamuddin's village and the tomb garden; nobles' compounds have red sandstone gateways and walled gardens.

outskirts.title: Tomb gardens and fields
outskirts.text: Walled gardens round nobles' tombs, wheat and sugar-cane fields, villages under the ruins of Firozabad.

periods.label: Shahjahanabad
periods.summary: Shah Jahan's new capital, built 1639–1648 on the river north of Firozabad: the red-walled fort of Qila-i-Mubarak with marble palaces on the water, the Jama Masjid on its rocky hill, Chandni Chowk with a canal down its middle, Faiz Bazaar, Jahanara's serai and garden, all ringed by a stone wall with fourteen gates. Aurangzeb has just taken the throne.
periods.feel: Elephants and palanquins in Chandni Chowk, the canal glinting under the trees, kettledrums from the Naubat Khana marking the hours.

houses.title: Havelis and katras of Shahjahanabad
houses.text: Nobles' havelis of brick and red sandstone round several courts, with zenana quarters and roof terraces; between them, mohallas and katras (gated markets with shops below, rooms above) reached by narrow kuchas closed by wooden gates at night.

outskirts.title: Suburbs and gardens
outskirts.text: Walled gardens of princesses and nobles, grain markets at Paharganj and Sabzi Mandi, potters, washermen and herders' hamlets beyond the walls.

periods.label: Zafar's Delhi
periods.summary: The British have held Delhi since 1803; the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, a poet, keeps court in the Red Fort on a pension, watched by a British Agent. Delhi College teaches Arabic and English in the old Residency, Dara Shikoh's library; St James' Church, the Magazine and bungalows cluster by Kashmiri Gate, and the troops live in cantonments behind the Ridge. A bridge of boats crosses the Yamuna.
periods.feel: Mushairas by lamplight, pigeons wheeling over the rooftops, the church bell by Kashmiri Gate answering the azan.

houses.title: Mohallas of late Mughal Delhi
houses.text: Old havelis subdivided among families and tenants, katras rebuilt with stuccoed fronts, carved wooden balconies and doorways; behind Chandni Chowk lanes of two- and three-storey brick houses round tiny courts, roofs given over to kites and pigeons.

outskirts.title: Bungalows, gardens and lines
outskirts.text: British bungalows in walled compounds north of Kashmiri Gate, cantonment lines behind the Ridge, old Mughal gardens, villages and brick kilns.

landmarks.name: Red Fort (Qila-i-Mubarak)

humayun-1570.note: Open riverbank south of Islam Shah's Salimgarh: gardens, a few nobles' houses and the ghats where the Yamuna runs under the high ground.

shahjahan-1660.note: New and complete: the Lahori and Delhi gates, the covered bazaar, the Naubat Khana, the Diwan-i-Am, and marble palaces along the river wall joined by the Nahr-i-Bihisht. Aurangzeb's Moti Masjid is being built.

zafar-1850.note: Zafar's court on a British pension: Aurangzeb's barbicans veil both gates, the Peacock Throne left with Nadir Shah in 1739, and a new red sandstone pavilion stands in the Hayat Bakhsh tank.

landmarks.summary: Shah Jahan's palace-fortress on the Yamuna, built 1639–1648: red sandstone walls round marble halls of audience, private palaces and gardens, the centre of the Mughal empire until 1857.
details: Designed by Ustad Ahmad Lahori and Ustad Hamid and built in nine years, the fort is an irregular octagon about 950 by 550 m, walled in red sandstone that rises to about 33 m on the city side. The Lahori Gate opens on Chandni Chowk through a vaulted bazaar; beyond the drum house lies the Diwan-i-Am, and along the river wall the Rang Mahal, Khas Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas and baths, joined by the marble 'stream of paradise'.

The miniature shows the walls and bastions, both gates, the Chhatta Chowk, the Naubat Khana, the nine-arched Diwan-i-Am with its marble throne canopy, the riverside palaces, the Hayat Bakhsh garden and the Moti Masjid. Courts, lesser buildings and the hundreds of service quarters are simplified to blocks and lawns.

landmarks.name: Salimgarh

tughlaq-1380.note: A low island of sand and rock in the Yamuna, north of Firozabad's ghats.

surid-1545.note: Islam Shah Sur, Sher Shah's son, begins a rubble-walled fort on the island in 1546 to guard the river crossing against the returning Mughals.

humayun-1570.note: Humayun camped here in 1555 before retaking Delhi. A plain island fort of round rubble bastions, reached by boat.

shahjahan-1660.note: Joined to the new Red Fort by Jahangir's bridge of 1622. Aurangzeb is using it as a state prison.

zafar-1850.note: Part of the palace complex, a jumble of royal relatives' quarters and gardens. Zafar slips out through it in September 1857.

landmarks.summary: A rubble-walled island fort built by Islam Shah Sur in 1546, later the Red Fort's annexe and the Mughals' prison.
details: Islam Shah built Salimgarh to command the Yamuna crossing. Its thick walls of grey quartzite rubble, with round bastions, enclose an irregular island about 300 m long. Jahangir bridged the channel to the mainland, and the Mughals used it as a gaol for princes and nobles.

The miniature shows the bastioned rubble wall, a gate towards the Red Fort, a small mosque and barrack-like ranges inside. The plan and inner buildings are simplified; little is known of what stood inside before the 19th century.

landmarks.name: Jama Masjid (Masjid-i-Jahan-Numa)

humayun-1570.note: Bhojla Pahari, a low outcrop of rock above the scattered houses and graves north of Shergarh.

shahjahan-1660.note: Finished in 1656: the largest mosque in India, raised on the rock so that its domes and minarets stand over the whole city. Aurangzeb prays here on Fridays, riding from the fort.

zafar-1850.note: Still the city's Friday mosque; Zafar comes in procession for Eid. Book-sellers, cooks and kite-sellers crowd its eastern steps.

landmarks.summary: Shah Jahan's congregational mosque, 1650–1656, raised on a rocky outcrop: three marble domes, two striped minarets and three great stepped gateways.
details: Built by some 5,000 workers under the wazir Sadullah Khan, the mosque stands on a high plinth over the Bhojla Pahari. Flights of red sandstone steps climb to gates on the north, south and east (the royal gate, facing the fort). The court, about 100 m square with a central pool, holds tens of thousands; the prayer hall on the west has eleven arches and three white marble domes striped with black.

The miniature shows the plinth with its arcaded cells, the three stepped gateways, the arcaded court with corner pavilions, the prayer hall with its pishtaq, three onion domes and two minarets with three balconies each. Inlay is suggested by marble bands; the stairs are shortened.

landmarks.name: Chandni Chowk and the Kotwali

humayun-1570.note: Open fields and the lanes of a few villages north of the ruined Firozabad.

shahjahan-1660.note: New in 1650: the canal in its stone bed under shade trees, two-storey arcaded shops, and the Kotwali platform where the city magistrate sits in judgement.

zafar-1850.note: Roshan-ud-Daula's Sunehri Masjid (1721), with three gilded domes, stands beside the Kotwali; the canal, restored by the British in 1820, runs again. Shops now have stuccoed fronts and balconies.

landmarks.summary: The central stretch of Jahanara Begum's great avenue, with the canal down its middle and the Kotwali, the city's police and magistrate's court.
details: Laid out in 1650 under Shah Jahan's daughter Jahanara, Chandni Chowk ran about 1.3 km from the Lahori Gate of the fort to the Fatehpuri Masjid, 40 yards wide, the Nahr-i-Faiz flowing in a stone channel down its centre. The Kotwali stood on its south side; nearby the Sikh Guru Tegh Bahadur was executed in 1675.

The miniature shows a 300 m section: the canal and its trees, ranges of shops with flat roofs and arcades, the Kotwali chabutra and, in 1850, the small three-domed Sunehri Masjid. Shopfronts and balconies are generic; the exact line of the shops is not known.

landmarks.name: Jahanara's Sarai (Begum ki Sarai)

shahjahan-1660.note: The finest serai of the city, built in 1650 by Jahanara on the octagonal square: Bernier thought it like the Palais Royal. Persian and Uzbek merchants rest here with their horses and bales.

zafar-1850.note: Decayed but still standing; it will be demolished after 1857 and replaced by the Town Hall.

landmarks.summary: Princess Jahanara's two-storeyed caravanserai on Chandni Chowk, with arcaded rooms round a garden court, built in 1650 for travelling merchants.
details: Jahanara Begum, Shah Jahan's eldest daughter, built the serai with the square and garden behind it. Bernier and later writers describe arcaded rooms on two floors round a large court with a garden, and an arched gateway on the chowk; the number of rooms is not reliably recorded. It housed visiting merchants and ambassadors.

The miniature shows two storeys of arched rooms round a planted court, a tall gateway on the square, corner towers and a small mosque. The plan follows the usual Mughal serai; the building does not survive and its exact form is a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Fatehpuri Masjid

shahjahan-1660.note: Completed in 1650 by Fatehpuri Begum, one of Shah Jahan's wives, to close the western end of Chandni Chowk.

zafar-1850.note: Still a busy mosque among the grain and spice markets of Khari Baoli.

landmarks.summary: The red sandstone mosque that closes the western end of Chandni Chowk, built in 1650 by Shah Jahan's wife Fatehpuri Begum.
details: A single-domed prayer hall of red sandstone with seven arches, flanked by minarets, faces a court with a pool; ranges of shops and rooms enclose the court and a gateway opens east down Chandni Chowk.
The miniature shows the prayer hall with its fluted dome and pishtaq, low minarets, the court and gate. Proportions are approximate.

landmarks.name: Kotla of Firoz Shah

tughlaq-1380.note: Firoz Shah's palace-citadel on the river: walled courts, the Jami Masjid of Firozabad on its arcaded basement, a circular step-well, and the three-storey pavilion carrying the Ashokan pillar, gilded at its tip.
tughlaq-1380.name: Kushk-i-Firoz (the Kotla)

surid-1545.note: Sacked by Timur in 1398 and left by later sultans; Sher Shah's builders cart its dressed stone to Shergarh. The pillar still stands on its pyramid.

humayun-1570.note: A ruin-field of roofless halls and the bare mosque; villagers live among the walls.

shahjahan-1660.note: Quarried again for the walls of Shahjahanabad, just to the north.

zafar-1850.note: A picturesque ruin sketched by British visitors; James Prinsep had read the pillar's Brahmi inscription in 1837, the key to Ashoka's edicts.

landmarks.summary: Firoz Shah Tughlaq's palace-citadel of Firozabad (1354), with the mosque, step-well and stepped pavilion carrying a 3rd-century BCE pillar of Ashoka.
details: Firoz founded Firozabad in 1354. In the Kotla, a three-storey arcaded pyramid of rubble supports a polished sandstone pillar of Ashoka, about 13 m high, which Firoz had brought from Topra near Ambala on a 42-wheeled carriage and by boat down the Yamuna. Nearby stand the Jami Masjid, where Timur prayed in 1398, and a circular baoli.

The miniature shows the walls and gates, the stepped pyramid with the pillar and its gilded finial, the mosque on its arcaded undercroft, the baoli and palace ranges. The ruin variant takes off roofs and upper storeys. The palace buildings are conjectural.

landmarks.name: Kalan Masjid

tughlaq-1380.note: Under construction for Khan-i-Jahan Junan Shah, Firoz's prime minister; finished 1387. Rubble and lime plaster, whitewashed.

surid-1545.note: Still in use for the mohalla round it, among half-empty suburbs.

humayun-1570.note: A village mosque in the fields north of the old Kotla.

shahjahan-1660.note: Now inside the walls of Shahjahanabad, near the Turkman Gate; the black-washed walls give it its other name, Kali Masjid.

zafar-1850.note: A neighbourhood mosque in the dense mohallas near Turkman Gate.

landmarks.summary: One of seven mosques built by Firoz Shah's prime minister Khan-i-Jahan, finished in 1387: a fortress-like Tughlaq mosque on a high basement.
details: Raised on a storey of arched cells, the mosque is reached by a steep stair through a domed gateway. Its walls batter inward like a fort and the corners carry tapering towers. Inside, arcaded cloisters roofed with many small domes surround a court.
The miniature shows the plinth, gateway stair, battered walls with corner turrets, and the grid of small domes over the cloisters and prayer hall.

landmarks.name: Pir Ghaib and the Kushk-i-Shikar

tughlaq-1380.name: Kushk-i-Shikar
tughlaq-1380.note: Firoz Shah's hunting palace on the Ridge, with a second Ashokan pillar (from Meerut) set up nearby.

surid-1545.note: A deserted lodge on the Ridge, used by herdsmen.

humayun-1570.note: Known as Pir Ghaib, 'the vanished saint', after a holy man said to have disappeared here.

shahjahan-1660.note: A ruin in the scrub above the new city's gardens. The Meerut pillar will be broken by a gunpowder explosion under Farrukhsiyar (1713–19).

zafar-1850.note: Beside Hindu Rao's house; the pieces of the broken Meerut pillar lie nearby and will be set up again in the 1860s. In 1857 the Ridge pickets use the ruin.

landmarks.summary: A two-storey rubble building of Firoz Shah's hunting palace on the Ridge, possibly an observatory, near the second Ashokan pillar he brought to Delhi.
details: The Kushk-i-Shikar ('hunting palace') or Jahan-Numa was one of Firoz's pleasure buildings on the Ridge. The surviving part is a two-storeyed rubble block with a cenotaph and a hollow shaft that may have been used for observing the stars.
The miniature shows the two-storey block with its parapet, a stair and the shaft. The use of the building is not known; 'observatory' is a guess.

landmarks.name: Purana Qila (Din Panah)

tughlaq-1380.note: The mound of Indarpat, held to be the Pandavas' Indraprastha, with a village on top and Firozabad's suburbs below.

surid-1545.name: Shergarh (Purana Qila)
surid-1545.note: Sher Shah's citadel: walls of grey quartzite trimmed with red sandstone and marble, three great gates, and his new mosque, the Qila-i-Kuhna; the Sher Mandal is rising.

humayun-1570.note: Humayun's last palace: he died after falling down the Sher Mandal's stairs in January 1556. The court has moved to Agra and the citadel is quiet.

shahjahan-1660.note: 'The old fort': the village of Indarpat has spread inside the walls, among the mosque and the Sher Mandal.

zafar-1850.note: Still a walled village; the British survey the mosque as a fine monument of the Afghan kings.

landmarks.summary: The citadel of Humayun's Din Panah (1533), rebuilt by Sher Shah Sur after 1540: massive walls, three gates, the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque and the octagonal Sher Mandal.
details: Humayun began Din Panah in 1533; Sher Shah, having driven him out in 1540, rebuilt the citadel. Its walls, about 18 m high, have three double-storeyed gates: the Bara Darwaza on the west, Humayun's Gate on the south and the Talaqi ('forbidden') Gate on the north. Sher Shah's mosque of 1541 has five arches richly inlaid in marble and coloured stone under a single dome.

The miniature shows the walls with round bastions and the three gates, the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque with its five-arched facade and dome, and the two-storey octagonal Sher Mandal with its kiosk. The village variant fills the interior with houses. Wall lengths are approximate.

landmarks.name: Sher Shah Gate (Lal Darwaza)

tughlaq-1380.note: Fields and suburbs of Firozabad along the river road.

surid-1545.note: New: the southern gate of Sher Shah's city, Shergarh, of red sandstone and grey quartzite, with shops in its walls.

humayun-1570.note: Still the gate of the town opposite the citadel; Maham Anga builds her madrasa beside it.

shahjahan-1660.note: A stranded gateway on the Mathura road, its city gone.

zafar-1850.note: A ruin by the road to Mathura, called the Lal Darwaza for its red stone.

landmarks.summary: The red sandstone southern gate of Sher Shah's Shergarh, facing the Purana Qila across the Mathura road.
details: A tall arched passage between two half-round bastions, built in red sandstone with grey quartzite, with domed kiosks over the parapet. Rows of cells along its sides are said to have been shops.
The miniature shows the gate block with its arched passage and bastions. The line of the city wall it belonged to is conjectural.

landmarks.name: Khair-ul-Manazil

surid-1545.note: Open ground beside the new Shergarh gate, opposite the citadel.

humayun-1570.note: New in 1561: Maham Anga's mosque and madrasa. In 1564 an archer shoots at the young Akbar from its roof as he rides past.

shahjahan-1660.note: Still a mosque, its madrasa cells let to travellers and villagers.

zafar-1850.note: A neglected mosque by the Mathura road; the madrasa rooms are half in ruin.

landmarks.summary: The mosque and madrasa built in 1561 by Maham Anga, Akbar's foster-mother, opposite the Purana Qila.
details: Maham Anga, the most powerful woman at Akbar's early court, built this mosque with a two-storeyed madrasa round its court. The prayer hall has five arches with a single dome over the centre; the gateway is of red sandstone. Its name means 'the best of houses'.
The miniature shows the gateway, the cells round the court and the prayer hall with its dome. Proportions are approximate.

landmarks.name: Humayun's Tomb

surid-1545.note: Riverside ground north of Nizamuddin's village, among a few earlier tombs; Isa Khan's tomb is going up nearby.

humayun-1570.note: Just completed: the tomb gleams in red sandstone and white marble in its new charbagh, with channels running and young trees.

shahjahan-1660.note: The dynasty's mausoleum: over a hundred Mughals lie in its plinth, among them Dara Shikoh, buried here in 1659 after his execution.

zafar-1850.note: The neglected garden is planted with vegetables and fruit trees. In September 1857 Bahadur Shah Zafar will take refuge here and surrender to Hodson.

landmarks.summary: The garden tomb of the emperor Humayun, begun in 1565 by his widow Haji Begum: the first great Mughal mausoleum, ancestor of the Taj Mahal.
details: Designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, the tomb stands on a 7 m arcaded platform in the centre of a walled charbagh divided by water channels. The building, of red sandstone outlined in white marble, has chamfered corners, tall arched iwans on each face, chhatris on the roof and a double dome of white marble rising to about 47 m.

The miniature shows the garden walls, the west and south gates, the walks and channels, the platform with its arcaded cells and the tomb with its iwans, kiosks and bulbous double dome. Trees and inlay are simplified.

landmarks.name: Isa Khan's Tomb

surid-1545.note: Being built in 1547–48 by Isa Khan Niazi, a noble of Sher Shah and Islam Shah, in his own lifetime.

humayun-1570.note: An older neighbour of Humayun's new tomb, its tiles still bright.

shahjahan-1660.note: A Surid noble's tomb in the shadow of the Mughal mausoleum; later, villagers will settle inside its walled enclosure.

zafar-1850.note: Houses of a small village probably already crowd the octagonal enclosure; they were cleared in the 20th century.

landmarks.summary: The octagonal tomb of Isa Khan Niazi, a Surid noble, built 1547–48 in an octagonal walled garden with a mosque.
details: An octagonal domed chamber is ringed by a verandah of three arches on each side, with a kiosk over each face and a band of blue and yellow glazed tiles. A three-bay mosque stands on the west side of the octagonal enclosure.
The miniature shows the enclosure wall, the tomb with its verandah, kiosks and dome, and the mosque. Tiles are suggested by coloured bands.

landmarks.name: Arab Sarai

surid-1545.note: Open ground south of the road to Isa Khan's tomb.

humayun-1570.note: A walled serai built for Haji Begum, said to house Persian (or Arab) men who came with her and worked on the tomb. The tall eastern gateway was added by Mihr Banu in 1611–12.

shahjahan-1660.note: The serai has become a village of craftsmen.

zafar-1850.note: A crowded village inside the old walls.

landmarks.summary: The walled serai built for the workmen and attendants of Humayun's Tomb, entered by a tall red sandstone gateway.
details: Tradition says Haji Begum brought 300 Arabs (more probably Persians) back from her pilgrimage and housed them here. The surviving eastern gateway, of red sandstone with marble and glazed tile decoration, carries an inscription naming Mihr Banu and the reign of Jahangir.
The miniature shows the gateway with its pishtaq, a stretch of the cell ranges and the corner of the enclosure. The serai's full plan is not reconstructed.

landmarks.name: Dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya

tughlaq-1380.note: The Chishti saint's tomb, repaired by Firoz Shah, beside his step-well and the Jamaat Khana mosque; Amir Khusrau lies at his feet.

surid-1545.note: A place of pilgrimage for Afghan and Mughal alike; the village of Ghiyaspur crowds round it.

humayun-1570.note: Faridun Khan rebuilt the tomb in 1562 with a marble verandah and dome; nobles now seek burial nearby, and Humayun's tomb rises beyond.

shahjahan-1660.note: Jahanara will be buried here in 1681 under an open grave of grass, as she asked.

zafar-1850.note: Emperors' graves crowd the enclosure (Muhammad Shah, 1748); Ghalib, who will be buried nearby in 1869, comes here for the qawwali.

landmarks.summary: The shrine of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya (d. 1325), with his step-well and mosque, the spiritual centre of Delhi through every dynasty.
details: Nizamuddin, the great Chishti saint, lived and taught here at Ghiyaspur; his baoli was dug in 1321–22 despite Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's ban on labour. The tomb was repaired by Firoz Shah and rebuilt in 1562 with a marble-arched verandah and a dome. Qawwals sing at the tomb every Thursday evening.

The miniature shows the walled step-well with its steps, the Jamaat Khana mosque, the tomb with its verandah and dome, Amir Khusrau's tomb and the courtyard. The early variant uses a plainer domed tomb, as the 14th-century building is not known.

landmarks.name: Zinat-ul-Masajid

shahjahan-1660.note: Riverside mansions of Daryaganj; Aurangzeb's daughter Zinat-un-Nissa will build her mosque here in 1707.

zafar-1850.note: The 'cloud mosque' on the river wall, its striped domes reflected in the water; the British will use it as a bakery after 1857.

landmarks.summary: The riverside mosque of Zinat-un-Nissa, Aurangzeb's daughter, built in 1707 and known as the Ghata Masjid for its cloud-striped domes.
details: Raised on a platform over the river wall of Daryaganj, the red sandstone prayer hall has seven arches and three bulbous domes striped in black and white marble, flanked by two tall minarets.
The miniature shows the platform, the court, the prayer hall with its striped domes and two minarets. Court and platform dimensions are approximate.

landmarks.name: Kashmiri Gate

shahjahan-1660.note: The northern gate, on the road to Kashmir, Lahore and the summer gardens; a single arch between bastions.

zafar-1850.note: Rebuilt by the British in 1835 with a double arch and a bastion with gun-ports. On 14 September 1857 sappers blow it open to start the assault.

landmarks.summary: The northern gate of Shahjahanabad, rebuilt by the British with a double archway in 1835 and stormed in the assault of 14 September 1857.
details: The gate faced north towards the road to Kashmir. In 1835 Robert Smith rebuilt it with twin arched carriageways, part of the British strengthening of the northern walls with bastions. In the 1857 siege a party under Lieutenants Home and Salkeld laid powder bags at its gate and blew it in.
The miniature shows the gate, its flanking walls and, in 1850, the double arch and the bastion. The Mughal form of 1660 is reconstructed from the other gates.

landmarks.name: Delhi Gate

humayun-1570.note: The ruined northern suburbs of Shergarh, by the road to the Kotla.

shahjahan-1660.note: The southern gate at the end of Faiz Bazaar, through which the emperor rides to the Jama Masjid's Friday prayer or out to the tombs.

zafar-1850.note: The gate on the road to the Kotla, Humayun's Tomb and Agra.

landmarks.summary: The southern gate of Shahjahanabad at the end of Faiz Bazaar, on the road to Agra.
details: A tall arched gateway of red sandstone between octagonal bastions, with a guardroom passage and battlements, built with the city wall in the 1650s.
The miniature shows the gate block, bastions and kiosks.

landmarks.name: Ajmeri Gate

shahjahan-1660.note: The south-western gate, on the road to Ajmer and the shrine of Muinuddin Chishti.

zafar-1850.note: Next to Ghaziuddin's madrasa, now Delhi College, just outside.

landmarks.summary: The south-western gate of Shahjahanabad, on the road to Ajmer.
details: A single arched gateway with bastions in the city wall, built in the 1640s–50s.
The miniature shows the gate block, bastions and battlements.

landmarks.name: Lahori Gate (city)

shahjahan-1660.note: The western gate at the end of Khari Baoli, on the road to Lahore; caravans from Kabul and Lahore enter here.

zafar-1850.note: The gate towards Sabzi Mandi; in 1857 the insurgents sally from it against the Ridge.

landmarks.summary: The western gate of Shahjahanabad, at the end of Khari Baoli on the road to Lahore; demolished after 1857.
details: Not to be confused with the Lahori Gate of the Red Fort. A gateway with bastions like the other city gates; it was pulled down in the later 19th century and its exact form is not well recorded.
The miniature reuses the form of the surviving city gates.

landmarks.name: St James' Church

shahjahan-1660.note: Gardens of nobles' mansions inside the Kashmiri Gate.

zafar-1850.note: Colonel James Skinner's church of 1836, the first in Delhi: a cross-shaped plan under a copper dome with a gilded ball and cross.

landmarks.summary: Delhi's oldest church, built 1826–1836 by Colonel James Skinner near Kashmiri Gate: a Greek cross under a central dome.
details: Skinner, the Anglo-Indian cavalry commander, vowed to build a church if he survived a battle. Designed by Major Robert Smith, it has a cruciform plan with three porticoes of Doric columns and a central dome on a drum. The ball and cross on top were shot full of holes in 1857.
The miniature shows the cross plan, porticoes, the drum and dome with lantern and cross.

landmarks.name: The Residency (Dara Shikoh's library)

shahjahan-1660.name: Dara Shikoh's library
shahjahan-1660.note: The library pavilion of Prince Dara Shikoh, Shah Jahan's scholarly heir, executed in 1659; his mansion passes to other nobles after his death.

zafar-1850.name: The Residency
zafar-1850.note: Remodelled for the British Residents after 1803 with a classical colonnade over the Mughal core; since the 1840s it has housed Delhi College.

landmarks.summary: The library pavilion of Dara Shikoh, built in the 1630s–40s, later the British Residency, its Mughal core hidden behind a classical front.
details: Dara Shikoh, who translated the Upanishads into Persian, kept his library here near the river. After 1803 the British Resident, David Ochterlony, took over the building and gave it a classical facade; in the 1840s Delhi College moved in, and later it served schools and offices.
The miniature shows a Mughal pavilion with chhajja and kiosks (1660) and the same block behind a columned verandah (1850). The Mughal form is a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Delhi Magazine

shahjahan-1660.note: Riverside mansions north of the fort.

zafar-1850.note: The great arsenal of the north, packed with guns, powder and cartridges. On 11 May 1857 its nine British defenders blow it up rather than surrender it.

landmarks.summary: The British arsenal near Kashmiri Gate, blown up by its defenders on 11 May 1857.
details: The Magazine held the largest store of arms and powder in northern India. When the Meerut mutineers entered Delhi, Lieutenant George Willoughby and eight men held it for some hours and then fired the powder; the blast killed hundreds outside and was heard at Meerut.
The miniature shows a walled compound with a gateway, storehouses and gun-sheds. The layout is simplified.

landmarks.name: Begum Samru's Palace

shahjahan-1660.note: The eastern part of Jahanara's garden, the Begum Bagh.

zafar-1850.note: Built about 1806 for Begum Samru, the Catholic ruler of Sardhana, in a slice of the old Begum Bagh; after her death in 1836 it is let, and becomes the Delhi Bank.

landmarks.summary: The Palladian mansion of Begum Samru, the dancing-girl turned ruler of Sardhana, built about 1806 in Jahanara's old garden.
details: Begum Samru, widow of the adventurer Walter Reinhardt 'Sombre', commanded her own army and was courted by Mughals and British alike. Her Delhi house, on a high basement with a columned portico and wide stairs, was a centre of entertainments.
The miniature shows the raised basement, the double stair, the Corinthian portico and the flat-roofed block.

landmarks.name: Ghaziuddin's Madrasa (Delhi College)

shahjahan-1660.note: Open ground outside Ajmeri Gate; Ghaziuddin Khan will build his madrasa and tomb here around 1690–1710.

zafar-1850.note: Delhi College was founded here in 1825 on the old madrasa's endowment; in the 1840s it moved to the old Residency by Kashmiri Gate. The red sandstone court still stands outside Ajmeri Gate.

landmarks.summary: The red sandstone madrasa, mosque and tomb of Ghaziuddin Khan outside Ajmeri Gate, where Delhi College began in 1825.
details: Ghaziuddin Khan, a general of Aurangzeb, built a two-storeyed ring of student cells round a court, a three-domed mosque on its west side and his own tomb in a marble screen. Delhi College, founded with British support in 1825, began here before moving to the old Residency in the 1840s; its teachers included Master Ramchandra, and its pupils included early Urdu modernists.
The miniature shows the gateway, the arcaded two-storey cells, the mosque and the screened tomb.

landmarks.name: Flagstaff Tower

shahjahan-1660.note: Thorn scrub and rock on the Ridge.

zafar-1850.note: A small castellated signal tower of 1828 on the Ridge. On 11 May 1857 the British women and children of Delhi crowd into it before fleeing to Karnal.

landmarks.summary: A small round signal tower of 1828 on the Ridge, where the British families of Delhi took refuge on 11 May 1857.
details: The two-storey tower, battlemented like a toy castle, carried a flagstaff for signalling to the cantonment. On the first day of the uprising terrified officers' families waited inside it in the heat before escaping north.
The miniature shows the round tower with its battlements, door, stair turret and flagstaff, scaled up for legibility.

landmarks.name: Hindu Rao's House

shahjahan-1660.note: Rocky scrub on the Ridge near Firoz Shah's ruined hunting lodge.

zafar-1850.note: A colonnaded mansion built for William Fraser, then bought by the Maratha nobleman Hindu Rao. In 1857 it is the key British battery post, held by the Sirmoor Gurkhas.

landmarks.summary: The mansion on the Ridge built for William Fraser and owned by Hindu Rao, the key British post in the siege of 1857.
details: Built in the 1820s or early 1830s for the eccentric Commissioner William Fraser (murdered in 1835), it was bought by Hindu Rao, brother-in-law of the Maratha ruler Daulat Rao Scindia. In 1857 Major Charles Reid's Gurkhas held it under constant fire for three months.
The miniature shows a flat-roofed classical house with verandahs on a terrace. The architectural detail is generic.

landmarks.name: Metcalfe House

shahjahan-1660.note: Gardens and fields along the river north of the city.

zafar-1850.note: Sir Thomas Metcalfe's house on the river, built in 1835, with a library of Napoleon relics and English pictures; it is sacked on 11 May 1857.

landmarks.summary: The riverside villa of Sir Thomas Metcalfe, the British Agent at the Mughal court, built in 1835 north of the city.
details: Metcalfe filled the house, which had deep verandahs and underground rooms for the hot weather, with Napoleonic memorabilia and ran his household by the clock. His 'Delhie Book' of paintings records the city before 1857.
The miniature shows a single-storey villa with a columned verandah round a raised block, on a terrace towards the river.

spots.name: Dariba Kalan
spots.summary: The lane of jewellers, pearl-merchants and silversmiths running from Chandni Chowk towards the Jama Masjid.
details: The name is usually explained as 'the incomparable pearl'. Shops a few feet wide open on the lane, the jeweller sitting cross-legged on a white sheet with scales and a strongbox; workshops behind and above beat silver into leaf, draw wire and set stones. Bankers and money-changers kept their counters here too.

vignettes.text: Shutters come down off the shopfronts; an apprentice sprinkles water on the dust and lays out the white sheet, the scales and the little brass weights.
A noble's steward haggles over a string of Gulf pearls while a silversmith upstairs taps out leaf for the sweetmakers, the beaten silver thin as breath.
Lamps in niches; the strongboxes are carried inside and the wooden gate at the end of the lane is barred for the night.

shahjahan-1660.note: New-built with the city; the court's jewellers and the Hindu and Jain bankers who lend to the nobles.

zafar-1850.note: Still the jewellers' lane; silversmiths make the silver leaf (varq) for sweets and paan.

spots.name: Kinari Bazaar
spots.summary: A narrow lane of gold and silver lace, braid and wedding trimmings off Dariba.
details: Kinari is the gold or silver border sewn on to a garment. Families of zardoz and gota makers worked here for the court and for weddings, wrapping metal strip round silk thread, and the lane still sells wedding finery. How early the lane took this trade is not certain.

vignettes.text: Spools of gold thread glint in the shade; a bride's mother unrolls a length of crimson brocade on the shop floor and runs a fingernail along the border.
A boy winds flattened silver strip round yellow silk at a wheel in the doorway, the coil growing on the spindle.
A wedding band rehearses in a courtyard behind; buyers squeeze past with packets of tinsel and mirror-work.

shahjahan-1660.note: Lace-makers working for the zenana of the fort and the nobles' households.

zafar-1850.note: Lace and tinsel for the weddings of the whole city; also kites and festival decorations.

spots.name: Ghantewala Halwai
spots.summary: The sweet-shop on Chandni Chowk said to have been founded in 1790 by Lala Sukh Lal Jain, famous for sohan halwa.
details: The name, 'of the bell', is explained either by the bell rung at the shop or by the emperor's elephant that would stop and ring its bell outside until fed. Both stories are traditions. The shop sold ghee-rich sohan halwa, karachi halwa and sweets for the court and the city until it closed in 2015.

vignettes.text: Ghee smokes in a wide iron karahi; the halwai stirs the sohan halwa until it crisps and sets in sheets studded with pistachio.
Servants from the fort queue for boxes of sweets wrapped in leaf, a tray of silver-leafed barfi glittering on the counter.
The last customers eat hot jalebis standing in the street while the canal murmurs beside them.

spots.name: A haveli in Ballimaran
spots.summary: A courtyard house off Chandni Chowk in Ballimaran, the quarter of physicians and poets, where Ghalib lived much of his life.
details: A carved stone gateway opens into a vestibule bent to keep out eyes, then a court with a neem tree. The men's rooms (mardana) face the court, the women's quarters (zenana) are behind; the roof terrace is for sleeping in the hot weather. Ghalib rented houses in this quarter; the haveli shown is typical, not his.

vignettes.text: The water-carrier's goatskin slaps on the courtyard stones; somewhere a hakim's pestle grinds herbs for the morning's patients.
Behind lowered chiks the household sleeps out the heat; a parrot in a cage complains to the empty court.
On the roof, friends lie on string beds under the stars and recite couplets to each other until the watchman calls.

shahjahan-1660.note: A noble's or merchant's haveli in a newly laid-out quarter.

zafar-1850.name: Ghalib's quarter, Ballimaran
zafar-1850.note: Mirza Ghalib, the greatest poet of the city, lives in rented rooms in this lane, writing letters and verses and gambling at chausar.

spots.name: Katra Neel
spots.summary: A katra, a gated market court with shops and storerooms, named after the indigo (neel) once sold there.
details: Katras were walled courts with a single gateway, shops on the ground floor and rooms above, built by nobles or merchants as investments and closed at night. Katra Neel became the cloth-dealers' quarter. The date and form of the first katra here are not recorded.

vignettes.text: The katra's gate swings open; bales of indigo-dyed cotton, still smelling of the vat, are carried in on porters' heads.
Brokers in white sit on the platforms with account books, calling prices across the court to the dyers.
The chowkidar locks the gate; dogs settle in the court among the empty bales.

shahjahan-1660.note: Indigo and cotton cloth traders round a walled court.

zafar-1850.note: Cloth merchants; English mill cloth begins to appear beside Indian weaves.

spots.name: A serai of Firozabad
spots.summary: A walled caravanserai on the road south from Firozabad, one of the many Firoz Shah is said to have built for travellers.
details: Afif credits Firoz with founding cities, forts, serais and wells across the realm. A serai was a square of cells round a court with a well and a mosque, its single gate shut at night, where merchants, pilgrims and soldiers slept beside their animals. This one is representative; its site is a guess.

vignettes.text: Camels groan to their feet in the court; a caravan for Multan loads up by lamplight before the gate opens.
The bhatiyari woman who keeps the cookhouse slaps out bread for travellers, a cauldron of lentils at her side.
The gatekeeper counts in the last travellers and bars the door; a storyteller begins under the arch.

surid-1545.note: Sher Shah's government repairs the serais on the great road, with a horse-post and a well at each.

spots.name: Bazaar of Firozabad
spots.summary: The grain and cloth market outside the Kotla's gates, where prices were fixed and famously low under Firoz.
details: Afif describes the abundance and cheapness of Firoz's reign. Markets were overseen by the muhtasib, who checked weights and measures. The exact site of Firozabad's main bazaar is not known.

vignettes.text: Grain-dealers heap wheat and millet on cloths; the muhtasib's man walks the row testing the weights in a brass pan.
Slaves of the sultan's workshops, some of Firoz's thousands, carry bolts of cloth to the palace stores.
Smoke of cooking fires; a bhishti sprinkles the dust before the Kotla gate.

spots.name: Urdu Bazaar
spots.summary: The bazaar between the Jama Masjid and the fort: first the camp market (urdu) of the army, later the street of booksellers and printers.
details: The camp market served the soldiers and retinues waiting on the fort; the language of its mixed crowds, zaban-i-urdu-i-mualla, 'the tongue of the exalted camp', gave Urdu its name. By the 1840s booksellers, calligraphers and lithographic presses worked in and around it; Delhi's first Urdu newspapers were printed in the city in these years.

vignettes.text: A calligrapher trims his reed pen and lays out a page of a divan; a boy rubs lampblack into ink on a stone.
The litho press thumps; damp sheets of the week's newspaper hang on strings to dry over the shop.
Students from the madrasas haggle over a secondhand Gulistan while the azan sounds from the Jama Masjid above.

shahjahan-1660.name: Urdu Bazaar (the camp market)
shahjahan-1660.note: Sutlers, armourers and cooks serving the troopers and grooms who wait on the fort.

zafar-1850.note: Bookshops, calligraphers and lithograph presses, the centre of Urdu publishing.

spots.name: Pigeon-fliers' rooftop
spots.summary: A rooftop loft of the kabutarbaz, the pigeon-fanciers who fly flocks over the city and try to lure each other's birds.
details: Pigeon-flying was a passion from the emperor down; Akbar kept thousands. Fanciers wave a long pole with a cloth to send up the flock and whistle it home; when flocks meet, birds that come down on the wrong roof are captured. Dargah Quli Khan describes the craze in the 1730s.

vignettes.text: The fancier throws open the bamboo loft and waves his flag-pole; two hundred grey and white birds burst over the roofs and wheel towards the river.
Two flocks mingle over Ballimaran; shouts and whistles from both roofs as each man tries to draw the other's birds home.
Grain scattered on the parapet; the fancier counts his birds in and croons over a captured stranger.

shahjahan-1660.note: Imperial and noble flocks; the emperor's pigeon-masters are paid from the treasury.

zafar-1850.note: Pigeon-flying is still a passion of every class, from the palace to the mohallas.

spots.name: A public hammam
spots.summary: A domed bath-house near the Jama Masjid, with hot, warm and cold rooms heated from a furnace below.
details: The fort had its own marble hammam, and nobles had baths in their havelis; public hammams served the city. A typical one had a dressing hall, a warm room and a hot room with a tank, under small domes pierced with glass lights. The location shown is representative.

vignettes.text: The stoker feeds dung-cake and wood into the furnace; steam already curls from the dome lights.
A masseur cracks a customer's joints on the hot slab, then sluices him with scented water from a brass bowl.
Friends linger in the cool hall over sherbet before the evening prayer.

spots.name: Nizamuddin's langar and qawwals
spots.summary: The kitchen and the singing courtyard of the dargah, where the saint's free food has been given out and qawwali sung for seven centuries.
details: Nizamuddin's hospice fed all comers; Amir Khusrau, his disciple, is credited with shaping qawwali. On Thursday evenings and at the urs the courtyard fills with pilgrims, Hindu and Muslim, while qawwals sing Khusrau's verses to drum and clapping (the harmonium came much later).

vignettes.text: Great copper degs of rice and lentils simmer over wood fires; the cooks stir with paddles as long as oars.
Pilgrims sit in rows on the ground while servers ladle out food; beggars and nobles eat the same.
Lamps on the tomb; the qawwals begin Khusrau's 'Chhap tilak', clapping rising until a listener falls into ecstasy.

tughlaq-1380.note: Firoz Shah endows the shrine; the khanqah still feeds the poor as in the saint's lifetime.

shahjahan-1660.note: Princes and princesses visit; Jahanara will choose to be buried here.

zafar-1850.note: Dargah Quli Khan described its crowds in the 1730s; the Thursday qawwali and the urs still draw the whole city.

spots.name: Agrasen ki Baoli
spots.summary: A deep stepped well of rubble, 60 m long, with arcaded sides descending a hundred-odd steps to the water.
details: Tradition credits the legendary king Agrasen; the masonry suggests a Tughlaq or Lodi rebuilding, so its date is uncertain. Stepwells kept water through the dry season and their shaded galleries were a cool place to rest.

vignettes.text: Women with brass pots descend the steps in single file; the water at the bottom is cold and dark.
Herdsmen doze in the arched niches out of the heat while boys dive from the lower landing.
Bats pour out of the shaft into the dusk.

tughlaq-1380.note: Perhaps newly rebuilt in rubble and lime, the usual Tughlaq masonry.

zafar-1850.note: A neglected well among fields and kilns south-west of the city.

spots.name: Nigambodh Ghat
spots.summary: The oldest and holiest bathing and cremation ghat of Delhi, on the Yamuna north of the fort.
details: Hindu tradition links the ghat to the Mahabharata; it has been Delhi's principal cremation ground for centuries. In Shahjahanabad it lay outside the Nigambodh Gate. Boats ferried pilgrims and goods along the river from here.

vignettes.text: Bathers wade into the river at first light, palms together, offering water to the rising sun; marigolds drift past.
Smoke from a pyre; a family sits on the steps while the Brahmin chants and a boatman waits for the ashes.
Oil lamps set afloat on leaf-boats bob away downstream past the fort's walls.

tughlaq-1380.note: A riverside ghat north of Firozabad's suburbs.

shahjahan-1660.note: Reached through the Nigambodh Gate of the new city wall.

zafar-1850.note: The bridge of boats lands just downstream.

spots.name: Raj Ghat ferry
spots.summary: A landing on the Yamuna below the city where ferries crossed to Shahdara and grain boats tied up.
details: Before the bridges, Delhi's river traffic used ghats and ferries along the west bank: grain, stone, timber and travellers came by boat. The landing below Daryaganj took its name from the Raj Ghat Gate of the city wall.

vignettes.text: The ferryman poles his flat boat off the sand, a buffalo and three farmers from Shahdara aboard.
Porters carry sacks of grain up from a moored barge, stacking them on the bank under a tarpaulin.
Dhobis spread washing to dry on the sand while the last ferry crosses against the sunset.

tughlaq-1380.name: Firozabad ghat
tughlaq-1380.note: Boats bring stone and grain to the Kotla; the Ashokan pillar itself is said to have arrived by river.

surid-1545.name: River landing
surid-1545.note: A landing among the ruins of Firozabad.

humayun-1570.name: River landing
humayun-1570.note: A landing among the ruins of Firozabad.

shahjahan-1660.note: Below the Raj Ghat Gate of the new city.

zafar-1850.note: The river has moved away; boats beach on a wide sandbank.

spots.name: Chhatta Chowk (the covered bazaar)
spots.summary: The vaulted arcade of shops inside the Red Fort's Lahori Gate, selling silks, jewellery and fine goods to the court.
details: Shah Jahan copied the covered bazaar from one he admired at Peshawar. Two storeys of arched shops line a vaulted passage with an open octagon in the middle. Within the palace, the court also held a Meena Bazaar, a fair at which ladies of the harem played at keeping shop for the emperor and nobles.

vignettes.text: Eunuchs from the zenana inspect Gujarat silks under the vault, while a perfumer uncorks attar of roses for a lady's maid.
Courtiers in from the Diwan-i-Am stop to buy jade cups and Kashmir shawls on their way out.
Lamps in the arches; the bazaar is closed as the Lahori Gate shuts and the guard changes.

shahjahan-1660.note: Luxuries for the court and the zenana.

zafar-1850.note: Shabbier stalls selling to palace residents and British visitors.

spots.name: The Kotwali
spots.summary: The office and platform (chabutra) of the kotwal, the city's chief of police and magistrate, on Chandni Chowk.
details: The kotwal kept the watch, the markets and the prices, collected news and punished thieves; offenders were displayed on the chabutra. The Sikh Guru Tegh Bahadur was executed near here in 1675. In 1857 the British hanged rebels in front of it.

vignettes.text: The kotwal's clerks read out the night's thefts; a watchman drags in a pickpocket caught at the Jama Masjid steps.
Shopkeepers bring a dispute over a short weight; the naib kotwal listens, then fines both.
Night patrols set out with lanterns and drums; the kucha gates are checked one by one.

shahjahan-1660.note: The kotwal answers to the emperor for the city's order and prices.

zafar-1850.note: Now under the British magistrate; still the police station of the city.

spots.name: Madrasa-i-Rahimiya
spots.summary: The theological school founded by Shah Abdur Rahim and made famous by his son Shah Waliullah, outside the Delhi Gate.
details: Shah Waliullah (1703–1762) translated the Quran into Persian and argued for reform; his sons, especially Shah Abdul Aziz (d. 1824), made the school the centre of Sunni learning in north India. Its building is not recorded in detail; the position is approximate.

vignettes.text: Students recite the morning lesson in a low hum, swaying over their books on the mat.
A teacher dictates a commentary on hadith; boys copy it in the shade of the colonnade.
Lamps in the cells; two students argue a point of law long into the night.

spots.name: Chawri Bazaar
spots.summary: The street west of the Jama Masjid, of brass and copper sellers below and, in the 18th and 19th centuries, the salons of courtesans above.
details: Dargah Quli Khan's Muraqqa describes the celebrated singers and dancers of Muhammad Shah's Delhi. By Zafar's time the courtesans' upper rooms in Chawri were where nobles and poets heard ghazals sung. The trade in metal vessels below was older.

vignettes.text: Coppersmiths hammer a cauldron in the street; stacks of polished brass lotas flash in the sun.
Tinners re-coat old pots over charcoal braziers, the smell of sal ammoniac sharp in the lane.
From an upper balcony a sarangi and a woman's voice: a ghazal of Mir, and the patrons' 'wah, wah'.

shahjahan-1660.note: Metalworkers and the lanes leading to Hauz Qazi.

zafar-1850.note: The salons of famous courtesans above the brass shops.

spots.name: Sher Shah's post station
spots.summary: A dak chauki and serai on the great road by the gate of Shergarh, where Sher Shah's mounted couriers changed horses.
details: Sher Shah built serais at intervals along his roads, each with a well, a mosque, separate lodgings for Hindus and Muslims, and two horses kept ready for the royal post. News is said to have reached him from Bengal in days. The site here is illustrative.

vignettes.text: A courier gallops in from the Agra road, swings down, and is up on a fresh horse before the dust settles.
The serai's Brahmin cook boils rice and water for Hindu travellers; the Muslim cook roasts meat on the other side of the court.
The drum at the gate beats curfew; the clerk enters the day's dispatches in his register.

humayun-1570.note: Akbar's government keeps the posts running along Sher Shah's road.

spots.name: Bu Halima's garden
spots.summary: A small walled garden with a tomb at the west approach to Humayun's Tomb, probably older than the great tomb itself.
details: Nothing certain is known of Bu Halima; the garden and its tomb are usually dated to the early 16th century. Visitors to Humayun's Tomb pass through it.

vignettes.text: A gardener lifts the sluice and water runs along the brick channel between the beds.
Masons on their way to the great tomb rest under the trees with their bread and onions.
Parakeets settle noisily in the tamarinds over the old grave.

surid-1545.note: A modest garden-tomb among the fields north of Nizamuddin.

zafar-1850.note: Overgrown; a village family grows vegetables in its beds.

spots.name: Qadam Sharif
spots.summary: The shrine Firoz Shah built in 1374 over the grave of his son Fath Khan, round a stone said to bear the Prophet's footprint.
details: The footprint stone, set in a tank of water inside a fortified enclosure, drew pilgrims for centuries; Dargah Quli Khan describes the crowds at its fairs in the 1730s. Around it grew a village, later swallowed by Paharganj.

vignettes.text: A keeper lifts the cloth from the footprint stone; pilgrims touch the water in which it lies and wipe their eyes.
Sweet-sellers and flower-sellers squat by the gate of the walled enclosure, shading their trays with cloths.
Lamps on the enclosure wall; a family sits by Fath Khan's grave reciting the Fatiha.

tughlaq-1380.note: New: Firoz's grief made monumental, a fortress-like enclosure in the fields west of Firozabad.

shahjahan-1660.note: A village of shrine-keepers outside the new city's western gates.

zafar-1850.note: Its annual fair crowds the lanes on the edge of Paharganj.

spots.name: Lal Mandir (Jain temple)
spots.summary: The red sandstone Jain temple at the fort end of Chandni Chowk, begun about 1656 for Jain soldiers and merchants of the Mughal army.
details: Tradition says Shah Jahan allowed Agrawal Jain officers to keep a tented shrine here, which became a permanent temple. It shows how the Mughal city mixed communities: Jain bankers and jewellers lived in Dariba and Kinari Bazaar close by.

vignettes.text: Worshippers in white with cloths over their mouths bathe the image and lay rice and almonds before it.
Bankers from Dariba step in between appointments, shoes left in a row on the steps.
Lamps are lit for the evening worship; devout families have eaten before sunset, as Jain practice asks.

shahjahan-1660.note: A modest shrine for Jain men of the army camp.

zafar-1850.note: Enlarged by the Jain merchants of the city; much of the present building is later still.

spots.name: Sabzi Mandi market
spots.summary: The vegetable market and market gardens outside the north-western gates, where growers from the villages sold to the city's cooks.
details: Sabzi Mandi lay among walled gardens on the Grand Trunk Road beyond the Ridge gap. In 1857 its gardens and serais became the battleground between the rebels' sorties and the British pickets on the Ridge.

vignettes.text: Bullock-carts creak in from the villages loaded with radishes, gourds and spinach still wet from the wells.
Cooks from the havelis haggle over baskets of mangoes, a porter balancing three on his head.
Rotten leaves swept into heaps for the cows; the gardeners count copper coins in the dusk.

zafar-1850.note: In 1857 its walls and gardens shelter the rebels attacking the Ridge.

spots.name: Paharganj grain market
spots.summary: The wholesale grain market in the 'hill market' outside Ajmeri Gate, which fed the capital.
details: Grain came in by cart and camel from the Doab and the Punjab and was stored in Paharganj's granaries before being sold on to the city's bazaars. Its banjaras (carriers) camped round it with their bullock trains.

vignettes.text: A banjara caravan of pack-bullocks, bells clanking, files in from the Ajmer road with sacks of wheat.
Weighmen sit by great balances, calling out maunds as porters pile the sacks.
Fires of the carriers' camp; dogs and bullocks settle among the stacked grain.

spots.name: Khuni Darwaza (Kabuli Darwaza)
spots.summary: The northern gate of Sher Shah's Shergarh, standing alone by the road south of Delhi Gate; later called the 'bloody gate'.
details: A tall gateway of grey quartzite with red sandstone trim, built about 1540. It took its later name from executions here; in September 1857 Hodson shot three Mughal princes beside it.

vignettes.text: Carts squeeze through the old arch on the way to the Kotla villages.
Goatherds shelter in the gate's shadow; a kite circles over the ruin-field beyond.
Travellers hurry past after dark; the gate has an ill name.

surid-1545.name: Kabuli Darwaza
surid-1545.note: The new northern gate of Shergarh on the road to Kabul and Lahore.

zafar-1850.note: Its grim name will be earned again in September 1857.

spots.name: A serai on the Agra road
spots.summary: A walled caravanserai among the ruins south of the city, where travellers on the road from Agra stopped before entering Delhi.
details: Mughal nobles endowed serais along the imperial roads; several stood on the stretch between Delhi Gate and Humayun's Tomb. The one shown stands for them; its site and name are not recorded.

vignettes.text: Bullock-carts for Agra rumble out of the gate in the dark; the gatekeeper takes his copper.
Horse-dealers from Kabul water their animals at the well and wash the dust from their beards.
Travellers spread their bedding on the platforms and buy bread and kebabs from the cookshop.

spots.name: Brick and lime kilns
spots.summary: Kilns in the open ground south-west of the city, burning brick and lime for Shahjahanabad's houses and walls.
details: Shahjahanabad was built of brick and rubble set in lime mortar, faced with red sandstone for the great buildings. Lime was burned from kankar nodules and limestone in kilns outside the walls; much stone also came from the ruins of the older cities.

vignettes.text: Smoke from a clamp of bricks drifts over the fields; moulders slap clay into wooden frames in rows.
Donkeys carry loads of fresh bricks towards the city gate, each one tapped by the buyer for its ring.
The kiln glows red in the dark; the burner sleeps beside it to tend the fire.

spots.name: Roshanara Bagh
spots.summary: The pleasure garden of Princess Roshanara, Aurangzeb's sister, north-west of the city; she was buried in its pavilion in 1671.
details: Laid out about 1650 in the formal Mughal manner, with walks, channels and a baradari, it was one of a ring of royal gardens outside Shahjahanabad, alongside Jahanara's Begum Bagh and the Shalimar further north.

vignettes.text: Gardeners clear leaves from the channels; peacocks call from the mango trees.
Curtained palanquins arrive: ladies of the princess's household come to picnic in the baradari.
The water in the channels darkens; a servant lights lamps in the niches of the pavilion.

zafar-1850.note: A quiet, half-neglected garden on the road to the Ridge.

events.title: Firoz Shah raises Ashoka's pillar
events.text: Afif describes the pillar wrapped in reed and raw silk, lowered on to a 42-wheeled carriage drawn by thousands of men, floated down the Yamuna on boats and hauled up the new pyramid with ropes and pulleys. No one in Delhi could read its inscription; James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi edicts only in 1837. The exact year is uncertain.

events.title: Khan-i-Jahan finishes the Kalan Masjid
events.text: Khan-i-Jahan Junan Shah, Firoz's prime minister and the son of a converted Telugu officer, completed this mosque, one of seven he built across the city. Its inscription gives the date. Its plinth of shops and fortress-like walls are typical of the late Tughlaq style.

events.title: Humayun founds Din Panah
events.text: Three years into his reign, Humayun chose the ancient mound of Indarpat for a new city, the 'refuge of the faith', and laid its first stone at an hour fixed by astrologers. The walls rose fast; seven years later Sher Shah had driven him into exile and taken the unfinished city for his own.

events.title: Sher Shah builds his mosque
events.text: Inside the rebuilt citadel Sher Shah raised a congregational mosque of five arched bays, faced with red sandstone and inlaid with white marble, black slate and yellow stone round its arches, under a single dome. It marks the step between Lodi and Mughal building.

events.title: Humayun falls on the library stairs
events.text: Six months after recovering his throne, Humayun was on the roof of the Sher Mandal, his library, when he heard the call to prayer. Starting down the steep stair to kneel, he caught his foot in his robe, fell headlong and struck his head. He died three days later; his death was kept secret until Akbar could be proclaimed.

events.title: An arrow at Akbar by Maham Anga's madrasa
events.text: Riding back from Nizamuddin's shrine, the young Akbar was struck in the shoulder by an arrow shot from the upper storey of Maham Anga's new madrasa. Abu'l-Fazl names the archer as a slave of the rebel Mirza Sharafuddin; he was caught and put to death on the spot. The wound healed.

events.title: Haji Begum begins Humayun's tomb
events.text: Humayun's senior widow chose a site by the river near Nizamuddin's shrine and engaged the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas. Red sandstone came from near Agra and marble from Rajasthan; the tomb took about seven years and is said to have cost 1.5 million rupees. Its double dome and garden setting became the pattern for the Taj Mahal.

events.title: Shah Jahan enters his new fort
events.text: Nine years after the foundation, the emperor came by river from Agra and entered the Qila-i-Mubarak by the water gate at an auspicious hour. The halls were hung with brocade and velvet and gifts were showered on the court. Delhi was again the Mughal capital.

events.title: Jahanara lays out Chandni Chowk
events.text: Shah Jahan's eldest daughter, the richest woman in the empire, built the octagonal square with its moon-reflecting pool, the serai on its north side and the garden behind. Bernier later called the serai one of the finest buildings of Delhi.

events.title: Aurangzeb's second coronation
events.text: Having imprisoned his father in Agra and defeated his brothers, Aurangzeb, already enthroned in haste in 1658 with the title Alamgir, 'seizer of the world', held a lavish second coronation in the palace. Within months he had begun the Moti Masjid in the fort and was tightening the rules of the court.

events.title: Dara Shikoh paraded through Chandni Chowk
events.text: Bernier watched the captured heir to the throne led through the city on a small, filthy elephant in a coarse dress, his son beside him, a guard with drawn sword behind. The crowd wept and cursed his betrayer. Within days Dara was condemned for heresy and beheaded; he was buried in Humayun's Tomb.

events.title: Nadir Shah's massacre
events.text: After a rumour of his death set the city on his Persian soldiers, Nadir Shah went to the Sunehri Masjid by the Kotwali and drew his sword: the signal for a massacre. In about six hours some 20,000 to 30,000 people were killed in Chandni Chowk, Dariba and the lanes, until Muhammad Shah begged for mercy. Nadir left with the Peacock Throne.

events.title: A mushaira at the court of Zafar
events.text: Bahadur Shah Zafar, himself a poet, held mushairas in the palace where Zauq, his ustad, Ghalib and Momin recited before the court, a candle passed from poet to poet as each took his turn. Rivalries between Zauq and Ghalib were the talk of the city; Ghalib became the court poet after Zauq died in 1854.

events.title: The Magazine is blown up
events.text: As the cavalry from Meerut and the city's own sepoys poured in, Lieutenant Willoughby and eight men held the arsenal, then fired the trail of powder. The explosion killed hundreds in the surrounding streets and shook the city; a few of the defenders escaped, burned and wounded.

events.title: The storming of Kashmiri Gate
events.text: After four months on the Ridge, the British assaulted at dawn. A party of engineers ran across the broken bridge under fire to lay powder at the gate; most were shot, but the charge blew the gate in and the columns poured through. Six days of street fighting and plunder followed.

events.title: Zafar surrenders at Humayun's Tomb
events.text: The 82-year-old emperor had fled the fort to the tomb of his ancestor. Captain William Hodson rode out, promised his life, and brought him back to the city as a prisoner; the next day Hodson shot three of his sons at the Khuni Darwaza. Zafar died in exile in Rangoon in 1862, the last Mughal.

stories.title: From Fatehpuri to the fort, 1660
stories.summary: A day's walk down the new capital's great avenue, from the western mosque to the emperor's hall of audience, early in Aurangzeb's reign.

steps.title: Fatehpuri Masjid
steps.text: Start at the red mosque that closes the avenue's western end, ten years old, its court full of traders from Khari Baoli washing for the noon prayer.

steps.title: Jahanara's square
steps.text: Walk east to the octagonal square: the moonlit pool, the princess's serai with Uzbek horse-dealers in its court, and her garden behind the wall.

steps.title: The Kotwali
steps.text: Pass the kotwal's platform, where a thief sits in the stocks and clerks write up the market prices for the emperor.

steps.title: Dariba
steps.text: Turn south into the jewellers' lane: white sheets, scales, pearls, and bankers counting rupees for a noble's debts.

steps.title: Jama Masjid
steps.text: Climb the steps of the new Friday mosque on its rock; from the east gate the whole fort lies across the bazaar.

steps.title: Chhatta Chowk
steps.text: Enter the Lahori Gate under its vault of shops, where silks and jade are sold to the court.

steps.title: The Diwan-i-Am
steps.text: Past the drum house, stand among the nobles behind the silver rail as Aurangzeb appears in the marble jharokha above.

stories.title: Zafar's Delhi, the last calm
stories.summary: Six stops through the city of Ghalib and Zafar a few years before 1857, where British and Mughal Delhi lived side by side.

steps.title: Kashmiri Gate
steps.text: Enter by the double-arched northern gate, rebuilt by the British in 1835, on the road from the bungalows of Civil Lines.

steps.title: St James' Church
steps.text: Skinner's church, its dome topped by a gilded ball and cross, where the British congregation meets on Sunday mornings.

steps.title: The Residency
steps.text: Dara Shikoh's library behind a classical colonnade: the first seat of British power in Delhi, and since the 1840s the home of Delhi College.

steps.title: Ballimaran
steps.text: Into the lanes south of Chandni Chowk, where Ghalib writes letters in a rented room and complains of his debts.

steps.title: Ghaziuddin's madrasa
steps.text: Outside Ajmeri Gate, the red sandstone court where Delhi College began in 1825 and its scholars first set about translating Western science into Urdu.

steps.title: Zafar's court
steps.text: Back in the fort at night, a mushaira: the candle passes from poet to poet before the old emperor.
